extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in early‑modern philosophy and essays
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and prescriptive remarks embedded in Montaigne's essay on the soul — skeptical reflections on knowledge, philosophers' errors, and how to present ideas. Useful for understanding epistemic and rhetorical guidance in early‑modern essaying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic humility
rubrics_metrics.description: Human judgment is fallible and limited; Montaigne repeatedly stresses our incapacity to attain certain knowledge (e.g., 'no human judgment is so sprightly and vigilant that it does not sometimes sleep').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confess ignorance where appropriate; avoid presumption. Montaigne endorses reliance on faith/divine assistance rather than overconfidence in unaided reason ('It was truly very good reason that we should be beholden to God only... Let us ingenuously confess that God alone has dictated it to us, and faith; for 'tis no lesson of nature and our own reason'). Use humility as a guide in philosophical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate reason by philosophers' errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge our estimate of human sense and reason by the manifest errors even among great philosophers ('Let us judge by these what opinion we are to have of man, of his sense and reason, when in these great persons... so many gross mistakes and manifest errors are to be found').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use collected examples of philosophical follies as a corrective to intellectual pride; treat famous authors' blunders as evidence of human limitation rather than purely as isolated mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid weak or silly reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Many philosophical arguments are either false or trivially silly (examples: Epicurean atoms needing hooked tails; Zeno making the world a mathematician or musician by facile inferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize argumentative moves for internal coherence and hidden assumptions; avoid superficial analogies and circular inferences. Montaigne highlights anti‑patterns (e.g., adding ad hoc hypotheses like 'hooked tails' to save an account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize clear, intelligible language
rubrics_metrics.description: When communicating, choose words that make you understood rather than striving for elegant correctness (advice: use the first word that comes to the tongue and adapt endings to local idiom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clarity and being understood across dialects or audiences rather than excessive refinement. Montaigne's pragmatic advice to an Italian learner is offered as an analogy for philosophical speech: adapt to your audience to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt presentation to audience ('concealment/adaptation of opinions')
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers sometimes disguise or temper their real opinions to accommodate public sensibilities ('They sometimes conceal their real opinions and judgments, and falsify them to accommodate themselves to the public use').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that rhetorical masking (poetic guise, moderation of claims) can be a deliberate strategy. As a producer of ideas, consider tailoring exposition so it is digestible; as a reader, be aware that surface statements may be rhetorical rather than literal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples of folly pedagogically
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting and exposing the absurdities of human wisdom is profitable and instructive ('Whoever should bundle up a lusty faggot of the fooleries of human wisdom would produce wonders... I willingly muster up these few for a pattern').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ counterexamples and humorous or striking errors to teach caution and humility. Montaigne treats such compilations as legitimate educational instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward popular consensus as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The consent of the many (popular belief) is not a sound foundation for metaphysical claims ('When we discourse of the immortality of souls, the consent of men that either fear or adore the infernal powers, is of no small advantage. I make use of this public persuasion' — presented critically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take widespread belief as substitute for reasoned proof; treat popular persuasion as psychologically explanatory but epistemically weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground claims in experience; avoid speculative excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that posit extensive unseen mechanisms (e.g., detailed accounts of transmigration, precise origins of sperm, or exact seat of the soul) should be treated skeptically when they outstrip observable evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanations tied to observable phenomena and be cautious about elaborate metaphysical constructions. Montaigne points out many competing, unresolvable accounts (seat of the soul, origins of seed, transmigration) to show the limits of speculative certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor moderation and avoid extreme conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers often fail by taking extreme, absolute positions; moderation and recognizing uncertainty are more defensible ('they tacitly lead us... to this resolution of their irresolution').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame claims with appropriate caveats, limit sweeping generalizations, and recognize alternative plausible views rather than insisting on absolute answers.
